title: Transplant status and rejection
question: Assign the ICD-10-CM codes for the patient's transplant status or transplant complication only.
note:
Chief Complaint
Follow-up for lung transplant status.

HPI
The patient is a 75-year-old male who presents today for a follow-up evaluation of his lung transplant. He reports a gradual increase in shortness of breath over the last three weeks, noting that he is becoming more fatigued during activities of daily living. He denies any acute fever or chills. He reports a persistent non-productive cough. He has been compliant with his current regimen of immunosuppressive medications but notes that his exercise tolerance has significantly declined since his last visit. He reports stable weight and no new symptoms of chest pain.

Review of Systems
Negative for fever, chills, night sweats, or productive cough. Negative for joint pain or rashes. Negative for changes in appetite or bowel habits. Positive for increased dyspnea on exertion and persistent dry cough.

Social History
The patient resides in a private home with his spouse. He retired three years ago and enjoys gardening and walking. He denies tobacco and alcohol use.

Family History
Father had hypertension and stroke. Mother had diabetes mellitus. Siblings are healthy.

Vitals and Recent Labs
BP: 132/84 mmHg, HR: 76 bpm, RR: 18 breaths/min, SpO2: 93% on room air, Temp: 98.6 F, Weight: 185 lbs.
Recent Labs: WBC: 6.4, Hemoglobin: 13.8, Platelets: 155, Creatinine: 1.1, eGFR: 72.

Medication List
Mycophenolate mofetil 1000mg BID
Tacrolimus 1mg TID
Prednisone 40mg daily

Exam
General: The patient appears in no acute distress but appears mildly fatigued.
Respiratory: Decreased breath sounds in the bilateral lower lobes. Auscultation reveals mild crackles.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. S1 and S2 are distinct. No murmurs heard.
Integumentary: No rashes or signs of skin breakdown.

Assessment
The patient is presenting with worsening respiratory symptoms following his lung transplant. Based on the clinical presentation and recent imaging, the patient is exhibiting signs of chronic lung allograft dysfunction. There is evidence of rejection.

Plan
1. Adjust immunosuppressive medications to address the rejection.
2. Increase Mycophenolate mofetil dosage.
3. Monitor tacrolimus trough levels weekly.
4. Follow up in two weeks for repeat imaging and laboratory work.

Electronically signed, H. Tanaka, MD, 05/14/2026
explanations: Rejection of transplanted lungs: lung transplant rejection, T86.810 (HCC 276).

distractors.why: A complication (rejection) is documented: use T86.810.
